title: The Uncle in the Subordinate Clause: Frankfurt, Altdorf, and the Four Rungs of a Free City
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Weikersheim an der Tauber, the name turned into Latin
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the source gives only 'around 1620, on entry into state service'; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: In the Hohenlohe town of Weikersheim an der Tauber the family is called Weber, weaver, and enters the service of the counts. On taking state office the name is put into Latin, Textor, and the German trade-word leaves the record. Wolfgang Textor, born 1588, rises to Hofkanzler, court chancellor of Hohenlohe, and dies in 1650. Every officeholder who follows in this line carries a scholar's surname that is really a craftsman's, and holds his office in the Latin the Empire keeps its law in. The trade the name was taken from is not practised by any of them again.
suggested_refs: The Hohenlohe chancery records of Weikersheim, where Weber becomes Textor

stops.name: Neuenstein in Hohenlohe, the jurist of the Synopsis is born
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Johann Wolfgang Textor is born at Neuenstein on the twentieth of January, grandson of the chancellor. He will write the Synopsis Juris Gentium, an early system of the law of nations, and hold chairs in two universities before a free city hires him. Three men of this family bear the name Johann Wolfgang, and secondary literature confuses them in one direction only, forward, toward the poet. This one is the poet's great-great-grandfather and the great-grandfather of Johann Jost Textor, who is not born for a hundred and one years.
suggested_refs: Johann Wolfgang Textor, Synopsis Juris Gentium (1680)

stops.name: Altdorf bei Nuremberg, the chair of law
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of appointment; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He is made professor of law at the university of Altdorf, in the Nuremberg territory, and moves on to Heidelberg from 1673 to 1690. The Altdorf lecture halls become the family's second address: his grandson reads law in them from 1712, his great-grandson takes a doctorate in them in 1760. The university answers to the Nuremberg council rather than to a prince, and it trains jurists for the imperial free towns, which is the employment this family lives by.
suggested_refs: The law faculty of the Universität Altdorf under the Nuremberg council

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Syndicus primarius arrives
stops.date_confidence: attested for early 1691; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Frankfurt engages him as Syndicus primarius, Konsulent and Stadtadvokat, and a Hohenlohe line becomes a Frankfurt line. The Syndicus is the council's own lawyer, appointed and salaried rather than elected. The free city crowns emperors and clears bills of exchange, and a closed circle of families supplies its councillors and its judges out of itself. The Textors are inside that circle from this year. His great-grandson will be elected to the same council eighty years on, and his great-great-grandson is Goethe.
suggested_refs: The office of Syndicus primarius in the constitution of the free imperial city

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Katharinenkirche, the first Textor grave
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He dies on the twenty-seventh of December and is buried in the Katharinenkirche, the chief Lutheran church of Frankfurt. The book on the law of nations outlives his name; in the city he is simply the first Textor of the place. The pastor of this church will marry his great-great-granddaughter to Johann Caspar Goethe forty-seven years on, and this parish is the likeliest to hold Johann Jost's own baptism, though no register entry has been found.
suggested_refs: The Katharinenkirche, evangelische Hauptkirche of Frankfurt am Main

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the next Johann Wolfgang is born
stops.date_confidence: contradiction not resolved: FPL node/1468 gives 12 December 1693, a separate encyclopedia extract gives 11 December 1693
stops.campa: A son is born to Christoph Heinrich Textor, judge in the Palatinate court, and Maria Catharina Appel, and is named Johann Wolfgang for the grandfather. He will govern Frankfurt for twenty-three years as its highest civic officer and be remembered chiefly because another grandson wrote about his garden. Of nine children he fathers, five reach adulthood and only one is a boy. That boy is Johann Jost, and the succession of a patrician house rests on him from the day of his birth.
suggested_refs: The Frankfurt baptismal registers of December 1693, where the day is at issue

stops.name: Altdorf bei Nuremberg, the second generation at law
stops.date_confidence: attested for the study years 1712 to 1717; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He matriculates at Altdorf and reads law there for five years, in the halls where his own grandfather lectured. The Textor pattern is fixed by this journey and will be run once more: Frankfurt boy, Altdorf jurist, Frankfurt officeholder. It is a circuit of two hundred kilometres, made out and back, once in a lifetime. For three generations of this family it constitutes the whole of travel, and no member of it is recorded going further in any direction.
suggested_refs: The Altdorf matriculation registers, 1712

stops.name: Wetzlar, admitted before the Reichskammergericht
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year, corroborated by a second encyclopedia extract; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He is admitted as advocate before the Imperial Chamber Court at Wetzlar, the supreme tribunal of the Holy Roman Empire, and afterwards takes his doctorate of law at Giessen. Wetzlar is where the Empire's lawsuits go to sleep for decades, and its advocates are paid to argue which court may hear a case rather than how it should end. This is as far from home as the practice of the line ever reaches. His son will never hold a posting outside Frankfurt at all.
suggested_refs: The Reichskammergericht at Wetzlar and its advocates' roll

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Römer, elected to the council
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the sixteenth of December he is elected to the city council. The year before, on the second of February 1726, he had married Anna Margaretha Lindheimer, born 1711, fifteen or sixteen at the wedding and eighteen years his junior; she outlives him by twelve years and buries him from the same house. The Rat is the lowest of the city's four ranks; the mayoralty, the Schöffenbank and the Schultheißenamt stand above it, and he is the only man of this family to hold all four in one lifetime.
suggested_refs: The Frankfurt Ratswahl records of December 1727

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, Friedberger Gasse, a daughter and the Schöffenbank
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of both events; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Catharina Elisabeth is born to the couple, and in the same year her father is made Schöffe, one of the magistrates who sit as the city's judges. The daughter will be the mother of Johann Wolfgang von Goethe and will be known across Germany as Frau Aja, on the strength of her letters. The office and the child arrive together in one year, and the office is the one the family expects to be remembered by. Her only brother is not born for another eight years.
suggested_refs: The Schöffenbank of Frankfurt, its bench and its rolls

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Römer, Elder Mayor
stops.date_confidence: attested for the three one-year terms of 1738, 1741 and 1743; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He serves as Älterer Bürgermeister, elder mayor of the free imperial city, for a one-year term, and holds it twice more, in 1741 and 1743. The mayoralty of Frankfurt rotates; the men eligible for it do not. Every election of his career has been held within a few hundred metres of the Römer, among the few hundred men who between them hold every office the city has to give. His son will hold the junior mayoralty forty-five years after this term, and never the elder one.
suggested_refs: The Frankfurt mayoral lists, 1738, 1741 and 1743

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, Friedberger Gasse, the only son
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; the family house is the father's documented residence, but no source states that the birth occurred in it
stops.campa: Johann Jost Textor is born on the twenty-ninth of September, the only son among the five Textor children who reach adulthood. His father is mayor of the city for the second time in his life. The family house stands in the Neustadt on the Friedberger Gasse, with the walled garden where an old man trains peach trees and a grandson will remember them being trained. The house is pulled down in 1863 and a hotel now stands on the ground. No source consulted says the birth itself happened inside it.
suggested_refs: The Textor house on the Friedberger Gasse, demolished 1863

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Katharinenkirche, a baptism not on record
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no baptismal register entry located, church chosen by confession and family use, day defaulted
stops.campa: A Lutheran patrician child of Frankfurt is baptized within days of birth, and the Katharinenkirche is the city's principal Lutheran church, the one this family uses. No register entry for Johann Jost has been found in any source reached for this journey. The church stands here as a reasoned guess, the entry itself as a gap. The Kaiserdom four hundred metres east, where emperors are crowned, stayed Catholic through the Reformation and is not a candidate.
suggested_refs: The baptismal registers of the Frankfurt Katharinenkirche, 1739

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Römer, the father made Reichsschultheiß
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the tenth of August the father is appointed Reichs- und Stadtschultheiß, imperial and city bailiff, the highest civic office Frankfurt has, held for life, and takes with it the title of actual imperial councillor. The son is seven years old. For the next twenty-three years the name Textor means, in this city, the man who presides over the court of the Schöffen. Johann Jost will hold three of his father's four offices and never this one. The bailiff's court sits in the Römer, a few streets from the family door.
suggested_refs: The office of Reichs- und Stadtschultheiß and its appointment of 10 August 1747

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the garden house of Johann Michael von Loën, the sister married
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; sources differ on the venue, and the coordinate for von Loën's country house outside the gates is approximate
stops.campa: Catharina Elisabeth Textor, seventeen, marries Johann Caspar Goethe, thirty-eight, a private gentleman of means with a purchased imperial councillor's title and no office. The pastor of the Katharinenkirche performs it, but not in the church: the ceremony is held at the garden house of the bride's uncle Johann Michael von Loën, on the Windmühle outside the city gates. Johann Jost is eight years old. He acquires a brother-in-law nineteen years his senior.
suggested_refs: The country house of Johann Michael von Loën, Auf der Windmühle

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the house on the Grosser Hirschgraben, the nephew
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Catharina Elisabeth bears a son in the Goethe house on the Grosser Hirschgraben and he is named Johann Wolfgang for his grandfather. Johann Jost, one month short of ten, becomes an uncle. The nephew's own life will carry him out of this house to Leipzig, Strasbourg, Weimar, Rome and back; the uncle's will not leave the Main valley except once, for a degree. The two houses stand a quarter of an hour's walk apart, and no letter between the two men survives.
suggested_refs: The Goethe house on the Grosser Hirschgraben, Frankfurt am Main

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Barfüßerkloster, the city Gymnasium
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no matriculation record for Johann Jost located, the year is a plausible schooling year, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The city's Gymnasium occupies the cloister of the dissolved Barfüßer convent and has done since 1542; the building comes down in 1838 and the Paulskirche is raised on the site. His father was schooled here, and his own son will be enrolled here in 1784. No matriculation entry for Johann Jost has been found here or at Altdorf in anything reached. That gap is stated plainly, and he is placed in the cloister on the strength of the two generations that flank him.
suggested_refs: The Frankfurt Städtisches Gymnasium in the Barfüßerkloster, 1542 to 1838

stops.name: Altdorf bei Nuremberg, the road east
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no matriculation date attested, mid-1750s inferred from the 1760 doctorate and customary ages of study, month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Somewhere in the middle of the decade he goes to Altdorf, two hundred kilometres east, a walled market town of the Nuremberg territory with a university inside it. No matriculation record for him has been reached. He is the third of his line to read law here, after his father and his great-grandfather; the family sends its sons to the place where its own dead once lectured. It is the only journey of his life that any source reached records.
suggested_refs: The Altdorf matriculation registers of the mid-1750s

stops.name: Altdorf bei Nuremberg, doctor of both laws
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day not given in any source consulted
stops.campa: He is promoted Juris Utriusque Doctor, doctor of both laws, the civil and the canon. The university will be dissolved in 1809 by King Maximilian I of Bavaria and its thirty-five thousand volumes carted to Erlangen, but the lecture building is not demolished: it stands, and houses a charitable institution. He is twenty or twenty-one, holds the highest degree the Empire's law faculties give, and turns west for home carrying it. No record of the disputation, its title, or its opponents has been reached.
suggested_refs: The Altdorf Kollegien- und Hörsaalgebäude, surviving as the Wichernhaus

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, admitted as advocate
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; no source names the place of admission, and the Römer is an assumption the atlas declines to make
stops.campa: On the sixteenth of June he is admitted to practise as an advocate in Frankfurt am Main. His father is Stadtschultheiß and presides over the bench before which he will plead. No source consulted remarks on this: the free city's constitution takes for granted that the same few dozen families furnish its judges and its advocates, and it is built to accommodate that rather than to prevent it. He is twenty-one years old, with thirty-one years of practice ahead of him.
suggested_refs: The advocates' roll of Frankfurt am Main, June 1761

segments.name: The Advocate in the Free City

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Kaiserdom, Joseph II crowned King of the Romans
stops.date_confidence: attested for the coronation; no source places Johann Jost Textor at the ceremony, and his presence is inference from residence and rank
stops.campa: The Empire comes to Frankfurt to crown Joseph II King of the Romans in St Bartholomew's, and the city spends weeks in scaffolding, wine fountains, and roasted oxen. A young advocate of a Schöffen family is in the town and in the class the ceremonial is arranged around; no source puts him at any particular point of it. His nephew, fourteen years old, watches the whole thing and writes sixty pages about it, in which the uncle does not appear. The uncle is twenty-four and three years at the bar.
suggested_refs: The coronation of Joseph II at the Frankfurt Kaiserdom, 3 April 1764

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Judengasse, the clients
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the atlas census names him as a Frankfurt lawyer with Jewish clients, no external source reached names a client or a case, and the date is a placeholder inside his years of practice
stops.campa: Tradition names Jost Textor, Goethe's kinsman, as a Frankfurt lawyer with Jewish clients in the city. Nothing in the Frankfurter Personenlexikon or the encyclopedias reached here names a client, a brief, or a fee. Any such clients would have lived in the Judengasse, the lane locked at night and on Sundays, a short walk from the Textor house. The claim stands here as tradition, the gap behind it left exactly as it is.
suggested_refs: The Frankfurt Judengasse and its Stattigkeit, the ordinance governing Jewish residence
sources: gap: no client, case or fee named in any external source reached

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the marriage to Maria Margaretha Möller
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; the church is a reasoned guess, no source names the venue, and the chronology stage of the research left this date blank while two other stages carried it
stops.campa: He marries Maria Margaretha Möller on the seventeenth of February. Five sons will come of it. Only one of the five can be dated from any source reached here, and the order of the others is unknown. Of the wife, the sources give a name, a wedding day, and a face: she sits for a pendant portrait beside her husband about the time he enters the council, and both canvases are still held by the Frankfurt Goethe Museum. No date of death for her has been found.
suggested_refs: The Frankfurt marriage registers, February 1766

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, Friedberger Gasse, the father's stroke
stops.date_confidence: attested for the month; day defaulted
stops.campa: In August the Stadtschultheiß suffers a stroke and is left partly paralysed. He is seventy-four and holds for life an office he can no longer discharge. The only son, twenty-eight and seven years in practice, takes up what the family cannot leave undone. In the same year, in the house on the Grosser Hirschgraben, the nephew comes home from Leipzig spitting blood and is nursed through a long convalescence by Susanna Katharina von Klettenberg, another kinswoman of his mother.
suggested_refs: The Frankfurt council minutes on the Schultheiß's incapacity, 1768 to 1770

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Römer, the office resigned
stops.date_confidence: attested for the month; day defaulted
stops.campa: After twenty-two months of trying to hold it from a sickroom, he resigns the Schultheißenamt in June on grounds of disability. The office was granted for life and he gives it back alive, which the constitution allows on grounds of incapacity and few holders have occasion to do. Frankfurt appoints a successor within the same closed circle. The Textor name comes off the highest office in the free city and never goes back on it in any generation. His son will sit in this building for twenty-one years and be given three of its four ranks.
suggested_refs: The resignation of the Schultheißenamt, June 1770

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, Friedberger Gasse, the father dies
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Johann Wolfgang Textor dies on the sixth of February, seventy-seven years old, thirty months after the stroke. He had presided over the Schöffen court for twenty-three years and grown peaches on a south wall. The grandson who will make the name famous is twenty-one and just home from Strasbourg with a licentiate in law and a head full of Herder. The only son is thirty-one, and is now, in the arithmetic of the free city, the head of the house. Between the two of them stands a woman who wrote more letters than either.
suggested_refs: The Frankfurt death registers, February 1771

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Peterskirchhof, the father buried
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no individual burial record located, the placement rests on the citywide rule and the documented Textor family plot, day defaulted
stops.campa: The Peterskirchhof outside the old wall, founded in 1508, takes every Protestant Frankfurter who dies until 1828, patrician and pauper into the same ground. The Textors hold a family plot in it. No burial record for the Stadtschultheiß has been located in anything reached. The rule is attested and the family plot is attested; the burial is not. He is placed there on the first two, the third marked as missing. Every Frankfurt Textor who dies before 1828 is subject to the same rule.
suggested_refs: The Peterskirchhof burial registers, February 1771
sources: gap: no individual burial record located

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Römer, into the council
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year, following the father's death in February; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The father is buried and the son is elected to the Rat. It is the only sentence the nephew ever writes about him: the uncle comes into the council and hands the young lawyer the small cases he can manage. Goethe is at that moment an advocate in his father's house, bored, drafting briefs between the first scenes of Götz von Berlichingen. In a life of twelve thousand printed pages this is the whole surviving record of Johann Jost Textor, given in a subordinate clause.
stops.quote: After the death of my grandfather, my uncle Textor had come into the council, and consigned to me the little offices to which I was equal; while the brothers Schlosser did the same.
stops.quote_source: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Truth and Poetry: From My Own Life, trans. John Oxenford (London: George Bell and Sons, 1897), Part Three; Project Gutenberg ebook 52654. The German original has not been collated.
suggested_refs: Dichtung und Wahrheit, Part Three, on the Frankfurt legal apprenticeship of 1771 and 1772
sources: Goethe, Truth and Poetry, trans. Oxenford (1897), Project Gutenberg 52654

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the pendant portraits
stops.date_confidence: attested as um 1771, about 1771; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: A pair of oils is painted, husband and wife, hung as pendants and attributed to Johann Volkmar Paderborn. They pass eventually to the Frankfurter Goethe-Museum, which holds them still. This is the whole of his iconography: no monument, no medal, no bust, no legend, one married couple on two canvases. The picture is the reason a face exists for a man of whom the archives keep four dates and four offices, and it hangs in a museum named for his sister's son.
suggested_refs: The Paderborn pendant portraits of Johann Jost and Maria Margaretha Textor, Frankfurter Goethe-Museum

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, Friedberger Gasse, Friedrich Karl Ludwig born
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the thirteenth of November a son is born, Friedrich Karl Ludwig, the only one of the five whose birth any source reached here can date. He will write as a schoolboy the earliest surviving comedy in the Frankfurt dialect, take a doctorate and a habilitation at Tübingen, teach there as extraordinary professor, come home, fail at the bar, and die in a charity hospital on the last day of 1851. His four brothers are not individually named in anything reached, and no source gives their birth order.
suggested_refs: Frankfurter Personenlexikon, 'Textor, Friedrich Karl Ludwig' (node/1465)

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the house on the Grosser Hirschgraben, the brother-in-law dies
stops.date_confidence: attested; an earlier stage of this research gave 30 May and put the death at the Textor house, which the sources do not support
stops.campa: Johann Caspar Goethe dies in his house on the Grosser Hirschgraben, seventy-one years old, after years of decline. His son is a minister at Weimar and does not come. His widow, Catharina Elisabeth, will live another twenty-six years in Frankfurt as the most celebrated letter-writer of the city. Her brother is a councillor of eleven years' standing a few streets away, and is presumed among the mourners; no source places him in the room. No letter between uncle and nephew has been found in any source reached.
suggested_refs: de.wikipedia, 'Johann Caspar Goethe', on the death of 25 May 1782

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Peterskirchhof, the Goethe grave
stops.date_confidence: attested for the burial ground and the year; the day of interment is not given
stops.campa: Johann Caspar Goethe is interred at the Peterskirchhof, in the same ground where the Textor plot lies. Two Frankfurt families that had married once are now buried a few paces apart under one wall. The cemetery will lose two thirds of its area to Prussian street-building and, in 1974, to the foundations of a diamond exchange, and where the graves exactly stood is no longer recoverable from anything above ground. The Textor stone, if it was ever cut, is not among the survivors.
suggested_refs: The Peterskirchhof, burial ground of the Goethe and Textor families

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Peterskirchhof, the mother dies
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of death; the burial in the family plot follows the pattern and is not individually recorded; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Anna Margaretha Textor, born Lindheimer, dies at seventy-two, twelve years a widow, and is presumed laid beside her husband. She had married at fifteen or sixteen, borne nine children, buried four of them, and lived to see her daughter's son become the most famous writer in the German language. Her only surviving son is forty-three and is about to be elected mayor of the city she was married into. Her burial in the plot is inferred from the family ground and the citywide rule, not from a record.
suggested_refs: The Peterskirchhof burial registers, 1783

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Römer, junior mayor
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He is elected Jüngerer Bürgermeister, the junior of the free city's two mayors, forty-five years after his father first held the elder office. Two years before, the presses of this city and Leipzig had jointly put out the first edition of Die Räuber for an army surgeon named Schiller who had run from Württemberg; in 1784 Kabale und Liebe opens at Frankfurt and Mannheim. The presses and the playhouse stand in the city he administers, and no source reached puts him at either.
suggested_refs: The Frankfurt mayoral list for 1783

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Barfüßerkloster, the son at school
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Friedrich Karl Ludwig, eight years old, is entered at the city Gymnasium, where the record notes that he attends irregularly. He will nevertheless leave that school with the manuscript of Der Prorector, a comedy in four acts in the Frankfurt dialect, the earliest such play that survives anywhere. It is reprinted in 1839 and again in 1893. Nothing his father wrote is known to survive, in print or in manuscript. His grandfather the Stadtschultheiß was schooled in this cloister; his father is placed here by pattern and by nothing else.
suggested_refs: The Frankfurt Gymnasium enrolment records, 1784

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Römer, the First Bank
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He is elected Schöffe and takes his seat on the Erste Bank, the senior bench of the city's court, the office his father held from 1731. Councillor, mayor, magistrate: three of the four rungs, in seventeen years, in one building. The fourth, the Schultheißenamt held for life, is not offered to him, and no source consulted comments on that or suggests it was expected. He has four years left to live and holds this bench for all four. His son is twelve years old and four years at the city Gymnasium.
suggested_refs: The Erste Bank of the Frankfurt Schöffengericht

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, Friedberger Gasse, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; no source names the place of death, and the family house is inference
stops.campa: Johann Jost Textor dies on the nineteenth of September, ten days short of fifty-three. He had been born in this parish, schooled in this city as far as anyone can tell, sent once to Altdorf for a degree, and had held three offices in one building for twenty-one years. The sources reached for this journey record no other travel of any kind: one imperial free city, one university town two hundred kilometres east, out once and back once. No cause of death is recorded in anything reached.
suggested_refs: The Frankfurt death registers, September 1792

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Peterskirchhof, the presumed grave
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no gravestone, register entry or burial notice for Johann Jost Textor has been located, the ground is inferred from the citywide rule and the documented family plot, day defaulted
stops.campa: Burial in Frankfurt is compulsory at the Peterskirchhof for every Protestant of the old and new towns until 1828, and the Textors hold a plot there. No gravestone, register entry, or burial notice for Johann Jost has been located in anything reached. He is placed in the family ground by rule and by pattern, which is how most of that century's Frankfurt dead are placed; the entry is marked as inference rather than record. No stone carrying his name is known to survive.
suggested_refs: The Textor family plot in the Alter Peterskirchhof
sources: gap: no individual burial record located

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, Der Prorector
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Two years after the father's death the son writes out Der Prorector, ein Lustspiel in vier Aufzügen, in the speech of Frankfurt's streets rather than the Saxon German of the schools. It is the oldest comedy in the dialect that survives. The family that turned Weber into Textor about 1620 to be admitted to the chancelleries produces, six generations on, a boy who writes in the vernacular the chancelleries were built to keep out. The play is printed again in 1839 and in 1893.
suggested_refs: Der Prorector, Ein Lustspiel in vier Aufzügen, reprinted 1839 and 1893

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the house of the wine merchant Gogel
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Gogel ownership of the house is attested elsewhere in the record; no document ties Textor's own descendants to it, and the date marks the general period rather than a fixed event
stops.campa: Five years after the Schöffe is buried, this house belongs to the wine merchant Johann Noe Gogel, one more Frankfurt patrician household among the many that pass in and out of the city's trading families within a generation. Private tutors keep rooms in such houses by the dozen in these years, hired and released with no more record than a name in a household ledger. Nothing in the family record ties Textor's own descendants to this particular house; it stands here only as one example of how such Frankfurt town houses changed hands.
suggested_refs: The Gogel house, Frankfurt am Main

stops.name: Tübingen, the son's chair
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of doctorate and habilitation, studies begun 1797; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Friedrich Karl Ludwig Textor takes his doctorate and habilitation at Tübingen, having gone up in 1797, and lectures there as Privatdozent and then extraordinary professor. It is the first move out of the Frankfurt and Altdorf circuit the family has made in a hundred and ten years. He comes back in 1813, opens a practice, closes it in 1816 for want of income, and lives afterwards by tutoring; one pupil is the dialect poet Friedrich Stoltze. He dies in a charitable hospital on the last day of 1851.
suggested_refs: The Tübingen habilitation records, 1800

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Peterskirchhof, Frau Aja in the family grave
stops.date_confidence: attested for the death and for the burial in the Textor family grave
stops.campa: Catharina Elisabeth Goethe, born Textor, dies on the thirteenth of September and is buried at the Peterskirchhof in the Textor family grave, not with her husband's people. Her son, fifty-nine and privy councillor at Weimar, does not attend. She is the last of that generation and the reason the ground is visited at all: the plot is now, in the city's memory, the Goethe mother's grave, and the brother in it, if he is in it, is unmarked. Her brother has been sixteen years dead when she is laid there.
suggested_refs: The Textor family grave at the Peterskirchhof, burial place of Catharina Elisabeth Goethe

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Peterskirchhof, the ground taken up
stops.date_confidence: dated to the attested last burial of 30 June 1828; the stop covers the losses that follow, the Prussian street-cutting through the nineteenth century and the 1974 diamond exchange, which are attested without individual dates
stops.campa: The last burial is Elisabeth Mauer on the thirtieth of June 1828, and afterwards the cemetery is built over in stages: Prussian street-cutting through the nineteenth century, and in 1974 the foundations of a diamond exchange, together taking about two thirds of the ground. Hans Backoffen's Crucifixion group of 1511 stands through it and is damaged by bombing in the war. From 1999 the surviving stones are conserved as an open-air museum, and since 1994 a piece of the retaining wall is the city's AIDS memorial.
suggested_refs: The Backoffen Crucifixion group of 1511 and the conserved stones of the Alter Peterskirchhof

stops.name: Frankfurt-Sachsenhausen, the Textorstraße
stops.date_confidence: attested for the extinction of the Frankfurt line with Karl Wolfgang Textor in 1925; the street coordinate in Sachsenhausen is approximate; month and day defaulted
stops.campa: The Frankfurt Textors end with Karl Wolfgang Textor, 1840 to 1925. Across the river in Sachsenhausen a street carries the name, and a primary school on it, and neither commemorates any one member of the family: the name is remembered as a name. There is no monument to Johann Jost Textor and no legend attached to him. There are two dates, four offices, five sons, one pair of portraits, and one subordinate clause in his nephew's autobiography. That is the whole surviving record of twenty-one years in office.
suggested_refs: The Textorstraße and Textorschule, Frankfurt-Sachsenhausen
